name: borrowing fire

attributes.attribute: Scottish and Irish ritual for keeping the hearth fire alive
the once-yearly night when the fire was allowed to die
tool that spins a stick in a plank to make sparks
gave the borrower power over the lender's cattle and wealth

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Borrowing fire is a Scottish and Irish ritual. In ancient times the hearth fire had to stay alive. The making of a new fire was arduous. Only once each year on Beltane Eve was the fire allowed to die. The next day it was relit from a festival blaze. If the fire died at any other time, the householder relit it. This work was done with a fire-drill. That tool spins a wooden stick in a small hole in a plank. The friction gives birth to sparks. Borrowing fire from neighbors was unlikely. People believed the act gave the borrower power. That power reached over the lender's cattle and wealth.

okr.objective: Explain the rule of the hearth fire and why borrowing fire was forbidden.
key_results: The hearth fire had to be kept alive in ancient times.
Only on Beltane Eve could the fire be allowed to die.
A fire-drill relit the fire if it went out at another time.
Borrowing fire was avoided because it gave power over the lender.
